bp: A web recommendation system is trying to follow a person whose interests are moving while the system is watching. Someone may start with travel photos, drift toward hiking gear, pause on restaurant videos, and later return to a destination guide. The platform sees interactions across several kinds of content, not only one list of products or articles. This paper serves that setting: recommending useful items when user interest is a path through time, shaped by text, images, videos, and links among users and items. The abstract argues that many recommenders freeze this path into separate snapshots or draw an over-simple line through it. That misses the fact that interest can move continuously and with direction. Drifting with Intent treats interest as something that changes moment by moment, then tries to generate a personalized trajectory that points toward meaningful content instead of treating future preference as a random next step.
wh: The hard part is that user behavior is both connected and time-sensitive. A click today may be a continuation of yesterday's topic, a short detour, or a sign that the user is leaving one interest for another. Multimodal platforms add another difficulty: items are not described by one signal. A video, image, caption, category, and past co-click pattern may each say something different about why the item matters. If the system records only discrete snapshots, it loses the motion between them. If it records only a simple trajectory, it may miss different granularities: one broad travel interest can contain narrower interests in flights, hotels, food, and outdoor gear. The abstract also contrasts directed drift with diffusion-style randomness. The tension is deciding whether the user's next interest should be modeled as wandering noise or as motion pulled by content that has relational and temporal meaning.
naive: A smart beginner would build a timeline of user actions, make one profile for each time window, and recommend items similar to the latest profile. That is reasonable because recent behavior often matters most. It fails in three ways. First, fixed windows cut a continuous process into artificial blocks, so the system may miss gradual movement. Second, one profile can average together several simultaneous interests, such as work research and entertainment browsing. Third, simple similarity to the latest actions treats all movement as local copying: show more of what was just clicked. The abstract's point is that interest has direction. A user is not merely near past items; they may be drifting toward a future content region that has not yet been clicked.
ap: The core idea is to model user interest as a continuous-time process with intent. Continuous-time means the model does not have to pretend that preference changes only at a few recorded timestamps. A stochastic process is a way to describe movement when the next position is uncertain; here it is governed by stochastic differential equations, which are rules for how a changing quantity moves while allowing noise. The paper's distinctive claim is that the movement is not just random spreading. It is directed drift toward meaningful content. To supply the map on which that drift happens, the method uses a multi-granularity hypergraph encoder. A hypergraph link can connect more than two things, such as a user, several items, and a shared context. Multi-granularity means it can represent broad and narrow interaction patterns. A unified solver then generates personalized interest trajectories across both time and relationships.
mech: The mechanism begins with user-item interaction records from multimodal web platforms. Each record is evidence that a user touched some content at some time, while the content itself may carry multiple media signals. First, the multi-granularity hypergraph encoder organizes these records into relational groups. At a small grain, it can capture specific user-item contacts. At a larger grain, it can capture cross-scale patterns, such as groups of users, items, and content types that repeatedly appear together. The encoder turns those groups into a structured state for the user: not a single flat profile, but a description of where the user's interests sit in a relational content map. Next, the model treats interest evolution as a continuous path through that map. The stochastic differential equation supplies the update rule: from the current state, one part describes intentional drift toward promising content regions, while another part leaves room for uncertainty because user behavior is never perfectly predictable. A unified SDE solver follows this rule across temporal and relational dimensions to generate a personalized trajectory. During training, the generative side learns to produce plausible interest paths, and the discriminative side learns to separate better recommendations from worse ones. The abstract says these are co-optimized in one parameter space, so generation and ranking precision are balanced without redundant twin networks. The output is both a ranked recommendation signal and an interpretable path showing how interests moved.
math: The main mathematical idea is a continuous-time stochastic process. In everyday terms, the model treats interest like a moving point whose exact future location is uncertain, but whose movement is not arbitrary. A stochastic differential equation is a rule for motion under uncertainty: it says how the current state changes over an infinitesimal slice of time, combining a directed push with random variation. The directed push is drift. In this paper, drift means the model believes user interest is being pulled toward meaningful content, not merely scattering in every direction. The second mathematical object is a hypergraph. A normal graph link joins two things; a hypergraph link can join a whole group. That fits recommendation because an interaction often involves a user, an item, a modality, a time, and a larger behavioral context together. Multi-granularity modeling is the idea that useful evidence exists at several scales, from exact contacts to broader clusters of related behavior. The third idea is co-optimization: deciding what counts as wrong for both trajectory generation and recommendation discrimination, then adjusting shared model settings so both errors shrink. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus discipline. A rich continuous path can describe subtle change, but it must remain tied to observed interactions and ranking goals.
dots: This paper belongs to the recommendation family because it addresses the repeated conference problem of choosing a small useful set of items from a huge changing catalog. It is specifically close to multimodal recommendation work such as the repo's MSCA record, which also worries that behavior and media content must be made compatible before ranking. The difference is that Drifting with Intent emphasizes movement through time, not only alignment among views. It also connects to graph-augmented recommendation records because the hypergraph treats relationships as carriers of evidence: neighbors and groups help explain where interest may move. It sits near sequential recommendation papers because the order of actions matters, but it pushes beyond a plain sequence by using continuous motion rather than isolated steps. Finally, it connects to generative recommendation because it does not only score existing candidates; it generates an interest trajectory that can be inspected as an explanation of why certain content becomes relevant.
ww: The method should improve over the naive snapshot approach because it preserves the thing snapshots destroy: motion. If a user's behavior gradually changes, a model with continuous time can represent the path between observations instead of treating each logged action as a disconnected update. The drift term helps because recommendation is usually not pure wandering. People follow purposes, moods, projects, and curiosity trails; the next useful item is often in the direction implied by several previous interactions, not just near the last clicked item. The hypergraph helps because interests are relational. A content item can be meaningful because of its image, text, co-viewed neighbors, and the user group that tends to choose it. Group links let evidence travel across those connected pieces without reducing every relationship to pairwise contacts. Co-optimizing generation and discrimination also matters. A generated path that looks plausible but does not rank good items is not useful, while a ranker with no path may be opaque and short-sighted. Training both goals together should make the trajectory both predictive and recommendation-relevant.
po: The payoff is a recommender that can treat user preference as a living trajectory rather than a stale profile. The abstract claims experiments across eight diverse datasets show better recommendation quality than state-of-the-art methods and produce interpretable interest trajectories. Grounded practically, that means a platform could recommend not only by asking what the user liked before, but by estimating where the user's interest is moving across content types and relationships. The interpretability claim is important: the system is meant to reveal how interests evolve, giving practitioners more than a ranked list with no account of the motion behind it.
limits: The abstract is truncated at the end, so some experimental and interpretation details are not visible in the provided input. The method assumes user interests really can be represented as continuous directed trajectories; if behavior is mostly erratic, coerced by interface exposure, or driven by one-time events, drift may give false structure. It also assumes the hypergraph captures meaningful cross-scale relations rather than popularity shortcuts. Multimodal signals must be relevant to user choice, and timestamps must be informative enough to support continuous-time modeling. The abstract reports eight-dataset gains, but it does not prove long-term user satisfaction, fairness, privacy behavior, serving cost, or stability when catalogs and user goals change rapidly.
